steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a game theory paper on search-and-rescue games played on a partially ordered set. Define the basic game, mention where these games came from and what they are used for, introduce the ordered and chained variants, explain the original game on a graph with its tree example, and end with the questions we study and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What a search-and-rescue (SR) game is
- Origins and applications; why order the locations (OSR and CSR games)
- Lidbetter's original SR game on a graph, and the tree example
- The tree example recast as an OSR game with correlated variables (Bayesian network)
- Motivating questions
- Organization of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## SR game
- two-player win-lose game on finite set X of locations
- Hider picks h\in X; Searcher picks permutation \sigma of X = a search
- if \sigma(j)=h: searched locations are \{\sigma(i)\colon i\leq j\}
- each x\in X has Bernoulli random variable \beta_{x}, distribution known to both
- Searcher wins (rescues) iff product of \beta_{x} over searched locations = 1; search halts once \beta_{x}=0
- payoff \Pi(\sigma,h) = probability of winning = rescue probability
- Hider wins if not rescued -> suicidal Hider

## Origins, applications, ordered variants
- first defined by Lidbetter; quickly fruitful
- applied to: scheduling problems, object detection, rendezvous problems, adaptive search
- natural to order locations: some jobs only after others have finished
- our setting: X a poset; search allowed only if \sigma(i)<\sigma(j) implies i<j -> ordered SR game (OSR)
- e.g. maximal m\in X with x<m for all x\not=m: search halts in m
- stronger: allowed only if i<j implies \sigma(i)<\sigma(j); such a function = chain -> chained SR game (CSR)
- Hasse diagram -> search game on (directed) graph, own topic
- search = path on Hasse diagram, may skip vertices, no backtracking -> appears to be new

## Lidbetter's original game
- (undirected) graph; Searcher picks path, Hider picks vertex h
- payoff = product of \beta_{v} over path vertices prior to h
- walk v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}; v_{j} first vertex equal to h; expected value of product of success probabilities
- \{v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\} is a multi-set; backtracking allowed; \beta_{x} sampled only once
- rooted tree, start at root -> Hider picks a leaf (internal nodes dominated)
- Lidbetter: optimal search = mix of depth-first searches
- example (from Lidbetter): rooted tree, three leaves a,b,c, one internal node; DFS at leaves: abc,bac,cab,cba
- h=a: abc gives \frac{1}{10}; bac gives \frac{1}{20}

## Tree example as an OSR game
- unordered X=\{a,b,c\}, correlated \beta_{a},\beta_{b},\beta_{c}
- nodes r,i = events deciding rescue: r = "no storm", i = "high visibility"
- a and b need both; c needs only no storm; plus own rescue probabilities depending on r,i
- tree = Bayesian network, r,i latent variables
- Pr(x)=Pr(\beta_{x}=1)
- Pr(a)=\frac{1}{10},Pr(b)=\frac{3}{20},Pr(c)=\frac{1}{3}; Pr(b|a)=\frac{1}{2},Pr(c|a)=Pr(c|b)=Pr(c|b,a)=\frac{2}{3} -> distribution determined
- recovers Lidbetter's tree game (only leaves searched); internal node probabilities = correlations between a,b,c

## Questions
- Lidbetter's depth-first theorem with other random variables?
- effective bounds on the value?
- ordered search?

## Organization
- notation and terminology
- solve CSR and OSR on a poset, uncorrelated Bernoulli; CSR harder despite smaller strategy space
- correlated variables: extend Lidbetter, link to Bayesian networks; bounds on value; solved only for simple posets with restrictions on the distribution
- final section: further generalizations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A search-and-rescue game (SR game) is a win-lose game between two players, played on a finite set X of locations. Hider picks a location h\in X and Searcher picks a permutation \sigma of X, which we call a search. If \sigma(j)=h then the set of searched locations is \{\sigma(i)\colon i\leq j\}. Each x\in X has a Bernoulli random variable \beta_{x}, and its distribution is known to both players. Searcher wins, i.e. rescues, if the product of \beta_{x} over the searched locations equals one, and otherwise she loses. So the search halts as soon as \beta_{x}=0. The payoff to Searcher \Pi(\sigma,h) is the probability that she wins, and we call this the rescue probability. Hider wins if he is not rescued, so we have a suicidal Hider.

SR games were first defined by Lidbetter and they quickly turned out to be a fruitful new area of study. They have been applied to scheduling problems, object detection, rendezvous problems, and adaptive search. In these applications it is natural to put an order on the locations, because some jobs can only be done after other jobs have finished. That is why in this paper we consider SR games on a partially ordered set X. Now a search has to respect the order, and it is only allowed if \sigma(i)<\sigma(j) implies i<j. For example, if m\in X is a maximal element with x<m for all x\not=m, then the search halts in m. We call this game an ordered search-and-rescue game, or OSR game. We also look at a stronger restriction, where \sigma is only allowed if i<j implies \sigma(i)<\sigma(j). A function like this is called a chain and we call this game a chained SR game, or CSR game. If the partial order is represented by a Hasse diagram we get a search game on a (directed) graph, and search games on graphs are a topic of their own. A search is then a path on the Hasse diagram where Searcher can skip some vertices but she cannot backtrack. She either searches a node or skips it, without turning back. This seems to be a new game on a graph.

- Lidbetter's original game: undirected graph; Searcher picks path, Hider picks vertex h; payoff = expected product of \beta_{v} over path vertices before h (walk v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}, v_{j} first equal to h); multi-set, backtracking allowed, \beta_{x} sampled once
- rooted tree from the root -> Hider picks a leaf; optimal search = mix of depth-first searches
- tree example with leaves a,b,c and one internal node; DFS abc,bac,cab,cba; h=a: abc gives \frac{1}{10}, bac gives \frac{1}{20}
- recast as OSR game on X=\{a,b,c\} with correlated \beta_{a},\beta_{b},\beta_{c}; r = "no storm", i = "high visibility"; Bayesian network with latent r,i
- Pr(a)=\frac{1}{10},Pr(b)=\frac{3}{20},Pr(c)=\frac{1}{3}; Pr(b|a)=\frac{1}{2},Pr(c|a)=Pr(c|b)=Pr(c|b,a)=\frac{2}{3}; recovers Lidbetter's tree game
- questions: other random variables? bounds on value? ordered search?
- organization: notation; CSR/OSR for uncorrelated Bernoulli (CSR harder); correlated case, Bayesian networks, bounds, simple posets only; generalizations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A search-and-rescue game (SR game) is a win-lose game between two players, played on a finite set X of locations. Hider picks a location h\in X and Searcher picks a permutation \sigma of X, which we call a search. If \sigma(j)=h then the set of searched locations is \{\sigma(i)\colon i\leq j\}. Each x\in X has a Bernoulli random variable \beta_{x}, and its distribution is known to both players. Searcher wins, i.e. rescues, if the product of \beta_{x} over the searched locations equals one, and otherwise she loses. So the search halts as soon as \beta_{x}=0. The payoff to Searcher \Pi(\sigma,h) is the probability that she wins, and we call this the rescue probability. Hider wins if he is not rescued, so we have a suicidal Hider.

SR games were first defined by Lidbetter and they quickly turned out to be a fruitful new area of study. They have been applied to scheduling problems, object detection, rendezvous problems, and adaptive search. In these applications it is natural to put an order on the locations, because some jobs can only be done after other jobs have finished. That is why in this paper we consider SR games on a partially ordered set X. Now a search has to respect the order, and it is only allowed if \sigma(i)<\sigma(j) implies i<j. For example, if m\in X is a maximal element with x<m for all x\not=m, then the search halts in m. We call this game an ordered search-and-rescue game, or OSR game. We also look at a stronger restriction, where \sigma is only allowed if i<j implies \sigma(i)<\sigma(j). A function like this is called a chain and we call this game a chained SR game, or CSR game. If the partial order is represented by a Hasse diagram we get a search game on a (directed) graph, and search games on graphs are a topic of their own. A search is then a path on the Hasse diagram where Searcher can skip some vertices but she cannot backtrack. She either searches a node or skips it, without turning back. This seems to be a new game on a graph.

The original SR game of Lidbetter is a game on an (undirected) graph. Searcher chooses a path and Hider chooses a vertex h. The payoff to Searcher is the product of all \beta_{v} over all the vertices v in the path before h. More specifically, let the path be a walk along the vertices v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n} and let v_{j} be the first vertex that is equal to h. Then the payoff of Searcher is the expected value of the product of the success probabilities. Here \{v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\} is a multi-set. Searcher is allowed to backtrack. If x occurs twice or more in the multi-set, \beta_{x} is still only sampled once. If the graph is a rooted tree and Searcher can only start from the root, then Hider selects a leaf, because all the internal nodes of the tree are dominated. Lidbetter proves that an optimal search is a mix of depth-first searches. For example, take the following example of a rooted tree with three leaves a,b,c and one internal node, which comes from Lidbetter's paper. In terms of arrivals at the leaves, the depth first searches are abc,bac,cab,cba.

If h=a and the depth-first search is abc, the payoff of Searcher is \frac{1}{10}. If the depth-first search is bac the payoff is \frac{1}{20}.

In our approach the SR game on the tree in Fig. 1 can be defined as an OSR game on the unordered set X=\{a,b,c\} with correlated random variables \beta_{a},\beta_{b},\beta_{c}. The nodes r,i are events that determine whether Searcher rescues or not. For example let r be the event "no storm" and let i be the event "high visibility". To rescue in a and b we need no storm and high visibility. To rescue in c we only need no storm. On top of that the locations a,b,c each have their own rescue probabilities, which depend on the events r,i. So the tree is a Bayesian network where r,i are latent variables. More formally, let Pr(x)=Pr(\beta_{x}=1) be the probability that the search of location x is successful. If we put Pr(a)=\frac{1}{10},Pr(b)=\frac{3}{20},Pr(c)=\frac{1}{3} and we put the conditional probabilities Pr(b|a)=\frac{1}{2},Pr(c|a)=Pr(c|b)=Pr(c|b,a)=\frac{2}{3}, then the probability distribution is determined. This gives back Lidbetter's game on a tree, where Searcher can only search the leaves. The probabilities of the internal nodes correspond to the correlations between the events a,b,c.

This raises some questions which motivate this study. What happens to Lidbetter's depth-first search theorem if the Bernoulli random variables are replaced by other random variables? Can we find effective bounds on the value of the game? And what happens if the search is ordered?

The paper is organized as follows. First we introduce notation and terminology. Then we solve the CSR and OSR games on a poset for uncorrelated Bernoulli random variables. The CSR game turns out to be more difficult to solve, which is surprising since its strategy space is more restricted. Then we look at correlated random variables, which extends the work of Lidbetter and links the SR game to Bayesian networks. We can give bounds on the value of the SR game, but we can only solve it for simple posets with restrictions on the probability distribution of the Bernoulli random variables. In the last section we discuss some further generalizations of SR games.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A search-and-rescue game, or SR game, is a two-player win-lose game which is played on a finite set X of locations. Hider chooses h\in X and Searcher chooses a permutation \sigma of X, which we call a search. If \sigma(j)=h then \{\sigma(i)\colon i\leq j\} is the set of searched locations. For each x\in X there is a Bernoulli random variable \beta_{x} with a distribution known to both players. Searcher wins (rescues) if the product of \beta_{x} over the searched locations is equal to one, and otherwise she loses. In particular, the search halts as soon as \beta_{x}=0. Searcher's payoff \Pi(\sigma,h) is the probability that she wins, which we call the rescue probability. Hider wins if he is not rescued, so we have a suicidal Hider.

SR games were first defined by Lidbetter in [1] and quickly proved to be a fruitful avenue of new study. They have been applied to scheduling problems [2,3], object detection [4], rendezvous problems [5], and adaptive search [6]. For such applications it is natural to impose an order on the set of locations, since some jobs can be performed only after other jobs have finished. In this paper we therefore consider SR games on a partially ordered set X. A search now has to respect the order and is only allowed if \sigma(i)<\sigma(j) implies i<j. For instance, if m\in X is a maximal element for which x<m for all x\not=m, then a search halts in m. We call this an ordered search-and-rescue game, or simply an OSR game. We also consider the stronger restriction that \sigma is only allowed if i<j implies \sigma(i)<\sigma(j). A function with this property is called a chain [7] and we call this game a chained SR game, or simply a CSR game. If we represent the partial order by a Hasse diagram, we get a search game on a (directed) graph, which is a topic of its own [8]. A search is a path on the Hasse diagram in which Searcher may skip some vertices but may not backtrack: she either searches a node or skips it, without turning back. This appears to be a new game on a graph.

Lidbetter's original SR game is a game on an (undirected) graph. Searcher chooses a path and Hider chooses a vertex h. Searcher's payoff is the product of all \beta_{v} over all vertices v in the path prior to h. More specifically, let the path be a walk along the vertices v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n} and let v_{j} be the first vertex equal to h. Then Searcher's payoff is the expected value of the product of the success probabilities. Note that \{v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\} is a multi-set, since Searcher is allowed to backtrack. Even if x occurs twice or more in the multi-set, \beta_{x} is still only sampled once. If the graph is a rooted tree and Searcher can only start from the root, then Hider selects a leaf, because all internal nodes of the tree are dominated. Lidbetter proves that an optimal search consists of a mix of depth-first searches. For instance, consider the following example from [1] of a rooted tree with three leaves a,b,c and one internal node. In terms of arrivals at the leaves, the depth first searches are abc,bac,cab,cba.

If h=a and the depth-first search is abc then Searcher's payoff is \frac{1}{10}. If the depth-first search is bac then the payoff is \frac{1}{20}.

In our approach, the SR game on the tree in Fig. 1 can be defined as an OSR game on the unordered set X=\{a,b,c\} with correlated random variables \beta_{a},\beta_{b},\beta_{c}. The nodes r,i correspond to events that determine whether or not Searcher rescues. For instance, let r be the event “no storm” and let i be the event “high visibility”. A rescue in a and b requires no storm and high visibility, while a rescue in c only requires no storm. On top of that, the locations a,b,c each have their own rescue probabilities, dependent on the events r,i. In this approach the tree is a Bayesian network [9,10] in which r,i are latent variables. More formally, let Pr(x)=Pr(\beta_{x}=1) be the probability of a successful search of location x. If we put Pr(a)=\frac{1}{10},Pr(b)=\frac{3}{20},Pr(c)=\frac{1}{3} and the conditional probabilities Pr(b|a)=\frac{1}{2},Pr(c|a)=Pr(c|b)=Pr(c|b,a)=\frac{2}{3}, then the probability distribution is determined. We retrieve Lidbetter's game on a tree, in which Searcher can only search the leaves. The probabilities of the internal nodes correspond to the correlations between the events a,b,c.

What happens to Lidbetter's depth-first search theorem if we replace the Bernoulli random variables by other random variables? Can we find effective bounds on the value of the game? What happens if the search is ordered? These are the questions that motivate this study.

The paper is organized as follows. We first introduce notation and terminology. We then solve the CSR and OSR games on a poset for uncorrelated Bernoulli random variables. Surprisingly, the CSR game is more difficult to solve, despite its more restricted strategy space. We then consider correlated random variables, extending the work of Lidbetter in [1] and linking the SR game to Bayesian networks. We are able to give bounds on the value of the SR game, but we can only solve it for simple posets under restrictions on the probability distribution of the Bernoulli random variables. In the final section we discuss some further generalizations of SR games.
